claim: COPD is one of the most common chronic diseases worldwide.
source: The prevalence of COPD, one of the most common chronic diseases worldwide, has been rising in recent decades (Mannino and Buist, 2007; thus, prevention and treatment of COPD are important issues of global healthcare.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mannino and Buist, 2007

claim: The prevalence of COPD has been rising in recent decades.
source: The prevalence of COPD, one of the most common chronic diseases worldwide, has been rising in recent decades (Mannino and Buist, 2007; thus, prevention and treatment of COPD are important issues of global healthcare.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mannino and Buist, 2007

claim: COPD bronchi are an area of intense immunological activity and tissue remodeling.
source: COPD bronchi are an area of intense immunological activity and tissue remodeling, as evidenced by the extensive immune cell infiltration and changes in tissue structures such as peribronchial fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about COPD pathology

claim: Distal airways are hypothesized to constitute a 'quiet zone' where exaggerated remodeling and inflammatory processes take place early in the disease history without identifiable symptoms or lung function test alterations.
source: In particular, distal airways are hypothesized to constitute a 'quiet zone,' where exaggerated remodeling and inflammatory processes take place early in the history of the disease, without identifiable symptoms or lung function tests alteration (Hogg et al., 1970; Mead, 1970).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hogg et al., 1970 and Mead, 1970

claim: Fibrocytes are fibroblast-like leukocytes produced by the bone marrow and released in the peripheral circulation.
source: Fibrocytes, fibroblast-like leukocytes, produced by the bone marrow and released in the peripheral circulation (Bucala et al., 1994), have been implicated in lung fibrosis (Pilling et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bucala et al., 1994

claim: Fibrocytes have been implicated in lung fibrosis.
source: Fibrocytes, fibroblast-like leukocytes, produced by the bone marrow and released in the peripheral circulation (Bucala et al., 1994), have been implicated in lung fibrosis (Pilling et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pilling et al., 2014

claim: Fibrocytes are recruited in the blood of COPD patients during an acute exacerbation.
source: They are also recruited in the blood of COPD patients during an acute exacerbation (Dupin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupin et al., 2016

claim: High circulating fibrocyte count during a COPD exacerbation is associated with an increased risk of death.
source: High circulating fibrocyte count during a COPD exacerbation is associated with an increased risk of death, suggesting that fibrocytes could be detrimental to the evolution of this disease (Dupin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupin et al., 2016

claim: Tissue fibrocyte density increases in COPD bronchi, which is associated with degraded lung function, increased wall thickness, and air trapping.
source: We have also demonstrated that tissue fibrocytes density increases in COPD bronchi, which was associated with a degraded lung function, increased wall thickness, and air trapping (Dupin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dupin et al., 2019

claim: Fibrocytes can function as antigen-presenting cells with T cells.
source: They can function as antigen-presenting cells with T cells (Chesney et al., 1997), which can in turn modulate fibrocyte differentiation (Abe et al., 2001; Niedermeier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chesney et al., 1997

claim: T cells can modulate fibrocyte differentiation.
source: They can function as antigen-presenting cells with T cells (Chesney et al., 1997), which can in turn modulate fibrocyte differentiation (Abe et al., 2001; Niedermeier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abe et al., 2001 and Niedermeier et al., 2009

claim: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells are predominant in the airways of COPD patients.
source: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells are predominant in the airways of COPD patients and their number inversely correlates with lung function (O'Shaughnessy et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Shaughnessy et al., 1997

claim: The number of CD8+ T cells inversely correlates with lung function in COPD patients.
source: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells are predominant in the airways of COPD patients and their number inversely correlates with lung function (O'Shaughnessy et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Shaughnessy et al., 1997

claim: CD8+ T cell-deficient mice are protected against lung inflammation and emphysema induced by cigarette smoke exposure.
source: CD8+ T cell-deficient mice are protected against lung inflammation and emphysema induced by cigarette smoke exposure (Maeno et al., 2007) whereas the expression of molecules linked to tissue destruction, such as perforin, granzyme B, and ADAM15, correlate with disease severity (Freeman et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2020), suggesting CD8+ T cells implication in lung inflammation and destruction in COPD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maeno et al., 2007

claim: The expression of molecules linked to tissue destruction (perforin, granzyme B, and ADAM15) correlates with COPD disease severity.
source: CD8+ T cell-deficient mice are protected against lung inflammation and emphysema induced by cigarette smoke exposure (Maeno et al., 2007) whereas the expression of molecules linked to tissue destruction, such as perforin, granzyme B, and ADAM15, correlate with disease severity (Freeman et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2020), suggesting CD8+ T cells implication in lung inflammation and destruction in COPD.
evidence: Supported by citations to Freeman et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2020

claim: Activation of CD8+ T cells is increased in COPD lung samples.
source: Activation of CD8+ T cells is increased in COPD lung samples (Roos-Engstrand et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roos-Engstrand et al., 2009

claim: CD8+ T cell activation could be partially T Cell Receptor (TCR)-independent.
source: Other studies have shown that CD8+ T cell activation could be partially T Cell Receptor (TCR)-independent (Freeman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Freeman et al., 2010

claim: The absence of increased expression of cytotoxic enzymes in peripheral blood CD8+ T cells from COPD patients argues in favor of local activation within the lungs.
source: The absence of increased expression of cytotoxic enzymes in peripheral blood CD8+ T cells from COPD patients argues in favor of a local activation within the lungs (Morissette et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morissette et al., 2007

claim: CD8+ T cells express an exhausted phenotype in the COPD lung.
source: CD8+ T cells express an exhausted phenotype in the COPD lung, that may result from an over-activation thus participating in the defective response to infection in COPD (McKendry et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKendry et al., 2016

claim: Fibrocytes derived from the blood of lung adenocarcinoma patients can strongly enhance the proliferation of CD8+ T cells.
source: A recent study showed that fibrocytes, derived from the blood of lung adenocarcinoma patients, could strongly enhance the proliferation of CD8+ T cells (Afroj et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Afroj et al., 2021

claim: The density of both CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes is increased within the subepithelial area of distal bronchi from COPD patients compared with control subjects.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Dupin et al., 2019; O'Shaughnessy et al., 1997; Saetta et al., 1998), the density of both CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes was increased within the subepithelial area of distal bronchi from COPD patients compared with that of control subjects (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A-C and citations to previous studies

claim: The density of CD8+ T cells in interaction with fibrocytes is higher in the sub-epithelial region of distal bronchi of COPD patients than in control subjects.
source: Whatever the magnification used to automatically count interacting cells, the density of CD8+ T cells in interaction with fibrocytes was higher in the sub-epithelial region of distal bronchi of COPD patients than in that of control subjects (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D-F

claim: The mean minimal distance between fibrocytes and CD8+ cells is significantly smaller in the sub-epithelial region of distal bronchi of COPD patients than in control subjects.
source: The mean minimal distance between fibrocytes and CD8+ cells was significantly smaller in the sub-epithelial region of distal bronchi of COPD patients than in that of control subjects (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G-H

claim: The mean minimal distances between CD8+ T cells themselves or between fibrocytes themselves are unchanged between control and COPD patients.
source: In contrast, the mean minimal distances between CD8+ T cells themselves or between fibrocytes themselves were unchanged (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B

claim: The density of clusters containing both CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes is higher in the distal bronchi of COPD patients than in control subjects.
source: However, the density of clusters containing both cell types ('mixed cell clusters') was higher in the distal bronchi of COPD patients than in those of control subjects, with a median number of 5 and 6 cells in these clusters in control and COPD tissues, respectively (Figure 1I–J, right panels).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1I-J

claim: Moderate but significant univariate correlations exist between the FEV1/FVC ratio and the density of fibrocytes, the density of interacting cells, the mean minimal distance between fibrocytes and CD8+ T cells, and the density of fibrocytes-CD8+ T cells clusters.
source: In particular, moderate but significant univariate correlations were found between the Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 s/Forced Vital Capacity (FEV1/FVC) ratio (used to diagnose COPD if below 0.7), and the density of fibrocytes, the density of interacting cells, the mean minimal distance between fibrocytes and CD8+ T cells and the density of fibrocytes-CD8+ T cells clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-D

claim: The best model for predicting FEV1/FVC associates the density of interacting cells and the density of mixed cell clusters, explaining 35% of the FEV1/FVC variability.
source: The best model associated the density of interacting cells and the density of mixed cell clusters. It explained 35% of the FEV1/FVC variability (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis described in the text

claim: Transcriptomic data reveal consistent changes in chemokines and chemokine receptors in COPD cells versus controls, mostly increases.
source: In contrast, transcriptomic data reveal consistent changes in COPD cells versus controls, mostly increases, in chemokines and chemokine receptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2A

claim: There are increases of CCL2, CCL26, CXCL2, and CXCL8 expression in tissue-resident memory CD8+ T cells from patients with COPD.
source: In particular, there were increases of CCL2, CCL26, CXCL2, and CXCL8 expression in TRM from patients with COPD, and CCL3L1 expression in TEM from patients with COPD (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The migration of fibrocytes is significantly increased by conditioned medium derived from tissular CD8+ T cells of COPD patients compared with those from control lungs.
source: The migration of fibrocytes was significantly increased by conditioned medium derived from tissular CD8+ T cells of COPD patients compared with those from control lungs (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The concentration of CXCL8 is increased in CD8+ T cells from COPD patients compared to control cells.
source: The concentration of CXCL8 was increased in CD8+ T cells from COPD patients compared to control cells (Figure 2D) in good agreement with the transcriptomic analysis.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Reparixin inhibits the increased migration of fibrocytes induced by the secretions of CD8+ T cells purified from COPD tissues.
source: Whereas fibrocyte treatment with reparixin had no significant effect on the control CD8+ T cells-mediated migration, it did inhibit the increased migration induced by the secretions of CD8+ T cells purified from COPD tissues (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 2E

claim: An anti-CXCL8 blocking antibody inhibits the increased migration of fibrocytes induced by the secretions of CD8+ T cells purified from COPD tissues.
source: Moreover, an anti-CXCL8 blocking antibody also inhibited the increased migration induced by the secretions of CD8+ T cells purified from COPD tissues, in the same extend than the blocking of CXCR1/2 by reparixin (Figure 2F), suggesting that this supplementary chemotaxis is mainly due to CXCL8 and not other CXCR1/2 binding CXCL chemokines.
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Tissular CD8+ T cells from patients with COPD promote fibrocyte chemotaxis via CXCL8-CXCR1/2 axis.
source: These data indicate that tissular CD8+ T cells from patients with COPD promote fibrocyte chemotaxis via CXCL8-CXCR1/2 axis.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of migration assays with reparixin and anti-CXCL8 antibody

claim: At the beginning of live imaging, nonactivated CD8+ T cells are equally allocated in fibrocyte-covered zones (41 ± 8%) and in fibrocyte-free zones (59 ± 8%).
source: At the beginning of live imaging, nonactivated CD8+ T cells were equally allocated in fibrocyte-covered zones (41 ± 8%) and in fibrocyte-free zones (59 ± 8%) (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: Twelve hours after the beginning of live imaging, most (77 ± 9%) of CD8+ T cells are present in contact with fibrocytes.
source: Twelve h later, most (77 ± 9%) of CD8+ T cells were present in contact with fibrocytes (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3A-B

claim: The mean speed of CD8+ T cells decreases upon contact with fibrocytes for both nonactivated and activated lymphocytes.
source: For both nonactivated and activated lymphocytes, the mean speed of CD8+ T cells decreased upon contact with fibrocytes (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3D

claim: A majority of intercellular contacts between CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes (49 ± 6% for nonactivated and 49 ± 8% for activated CD8+ T cells) are short-lived (<12 min) and dynamic.
source: Irrespective of the activation state of CD8+ T cells, a majority of intercellular contacts (49 ± 6% and 49 ± 8% for nonactivated and activated CD8+ T cells, respectively) were short-lived (<12 min) and dynamic, although some longer interactions (>32 min) could also be detected (30 ± 4% and 27 ± 7% for nonactivated and activated CD8+ T cells, respectively) (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3E

claim: There is a significant decrease in the mean speed for activated CD8+ T cells when they are in contact with fibrocytes compared to nonactivated CD8+ T cells.
source: However, we observed a significant decrease in the mean speed for activated CD8+ T cells when they were in contact with fibrocytes ('Mean contact speed') compared to nonactivated CD8+ T cells (Figure 3H), reflecting subtle behavior changes in this condition of activation.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The presence of fibrocytes in the indirect co-culture assay does not affect the proliferation capacity of non-activated CD8+ T cells.
source: The presence of fibrocytes in the indirect co-culture assay did not affect the proliferation capacity of non-activated CD8+ T cells and only moderately increased the number of dividing activated CD8+ T cells (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: Supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 3I-L

claim: In the direct co-culture model, the total number of CD8+ T cells and the percentage of dividing CD8+ T cells are far higher in the presence of fibrocytes irrespective of the activation state of CD8+ T cells.
source: In the direct co-culture model, the total number of CD8+ T cells and the percentage of dividing CD8+ T cells were far higher in the presence of fibrocytes irrespective of the activation state of CD8+ T cells (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: Supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 3M-P

claim: Direct interactions between CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes increase CD8+ T cell proliferation.
source: Altogether, this implies that a direct rather than indirect interactions between CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes increased CD8+ T cell proliferation, and that although fibrocyte-mediated effect on proliferation is not specific to CD8+ T cells, the extend of the effect is much larger on CD8+ T cells than on CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of direct and indirect co-culture results

claim: The inhibition of CD86 and CD54 significantly reduces the proliferation of nonactivated CD8+ T cells in the direct co-culture with fibrocytes.
source: The inhibition of CD86 and CD54 significantly reduced the proliferation of nonactivated CD8+ T cells in the direct co-culture with fibrocytes (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by blocking antibody experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Anti-CD86 and anti-CD54 blocking antibodies fail to alter the stimulatory activity of lymphocyte division by fibrocytes when CD8+ T cells are previously activated.
source: However, these antibodies failed to alter the stimulatory activity of lymphocyte division by fibrocytes, when CD8+ T cells were previously activated (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by blocking antibody experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: When nonactivated CD8+ T cells are indirectly co-cultured with fibrocytes, the expression of TNF-α and IFN-γ by CD8+ T cells is slightly increased.
source: When nonactivated CD8+ T cells were indirectly co-cultured with fibrocytes, the expression of TNF-α, IFN-γ by CD8+ T cells was slightly increased (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A-B

claim: Upon direct co-culture, there is a massive induction of TNF-α, IFN-γ, granzyme B, IL-10, and IL-17 in CD8+ T cells, irrespective of their activation state.
source: Upon direct co-culture, we observed a massive induction of TNF-α, IFN-γ, granzyme B, IL-10, and IL-17, irrespective of the activation state of CD8+ T cells (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: The concentration of TNF-α measured in culture supernatant increases significantly upon co-culture between fibrocytes and non-activated CD8+ T cells at day 4.
source: The concentration of TNF-α measured in culture supernatant increased significantly upon co-culture between fibrocytes and non-activated CD8+ T cells at day 4, confirming that TNF-α was secreted in the medium upon direct interactions with fibrocytes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Direct co-culture with fibrocytes increases total and membrane expression of the cytotoxic degranulation marker CD107a in CD8+ T cells.
source: Direct co-culture with fibrocytes increased total and membrane expression of the cytotoxic degranulation marker CD107a, which was only significant in non-activated CD8+ T cells (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A-E

claim: Following direct interaction with fibrocytes, CD8+ T cells have the ability to kill target cells such as bronchial epithelial cells.
source: This demonstrates that following direct interaction with fibrocytes, CD8+ T cells have the ability to kill target cells such as bronchial epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from increased CD107a expression and cytotoxicity assay results shown in Figure 6

claim: The top ten pathways most significantly activated in co-cultured versus mono-cultured fibrocytes include dendritic cell maturation, multiple sclerosis signaling pathway, neuroinflammation signaling pathway, and macrophage classical signaling pathway.
source: Of the top ten pathways that were most significantly activated in co-cultured versus mono-cultured fibrocytes, the largest upregulated genes were those of the dendritic cell maturation box, the multiple sclerosis signaling pathway, the neuroinflammation signaling pathway, and the macrophage classical signaling pathway, irrespective of the activation state of CD8+ T cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The proteomic changes in fibrocytes upon co-culture with CD8+ T cells are mostly driven by up-regulation of Major Histocompatibility Complex class I and II molecules, co-stimulatory and adhesion molecules.
source: They were mostly driven by up-regulation of a core set of Major Histocompatibility Complex class I (HLA-B, C, F) and II (HLA-DMB, DPA1, DPB1, DRA, DRB1, DRB3) molecules, co-simulatory and adhesion molecules (CD40, CD86, and CD54).
evidence: Supported by proteomic analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 7

claim: The interaction between CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes promotes the development of fibrocyte immune properties.
source: These changes suggest that the interaction between CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes promotes the development of fibrocyte immune properties, which could subsequently impact the activation of CD4+ T cells activation.
evidence: Inferred from proteomic analysis showing upregulation of immune-related pathways

claim: The computational model correctly accounts for the shift of the absolute and relative distribution of CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes in peribronchial areas from control subjects to patients with COPD.
source: Altogether, the theory of the influence of local interactions tested by our agent-based (cellular automata) model correctly accounts for the shift of the absolute and relative distribution of CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes in peribronchial areas from control subjects to patients with COPD.
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation results with experimental data

claim: The simulations predict that cell densities and their relative distribution are different between healthy and COPD situations.
source: Snapshots of the peribronchial area at the end of the simulations show that the densities of cells as well as their relative distribution were different between healthy and COPD situations (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8B

claim: The simulations predict a median of 754 CD8+ T cells/mm2 and 106 fibrocytes/mm2 in the control situation, and 1187 CD8+ T cells/mm2 and 212 fibrocytes/mm2 in the COPD situation.
source: From the simulations (n=160 in each condition), we found a median of 754 CD8+ T cells/mm2 (95% CI, 748–763) and 106 fibrocytes/mm2 (95% CI, 101–108) in the control situation, and 1187 CD8+ T cells/mm2 (95% CI, 1169–1195) and 212 fibrocytes/mm2 (95% CI, 206–216) in the COPD situation.
evidence: Supported by simulation results

claim: The relative organization of CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes in control and COPD bronchi does not result from a pure stochastic mechanism but implicates chemotaxis processes.
source: We conclude that the relative organization of CD8+ T cells and fibrocytes in control and COPD bronchi did not result from a pure stochastic mechanism but implicates chemotaxis processes.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of simulation results with random distributions

claim: Fibrocyte-induced T cell proliferation quickly increases in COPD situations over time to reach a plateau after approximately 4 years.
source: Fibrocyte-induced T cell proliferation, that represents the minor part of the total proliferation in control situations, quickly increased in COPD situations over time to reach a plateau after approximately 4 years.
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8H-I

claim: The density of mixed cell clusters gradually increases in the first years of the COPD simulation before reaching a stationary state after approximately 6 years.
source: The density of mixed cell clusters gradually increased in the first years of the COPD simulation before reaching a stationary state after approximately 6 years (Figure 8J, Video 2, Video 3, Video 4, Video 5).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8J

claim: An ideal treatment able to restore all cellular processes would reach levels similar to healthy subjects after approximately 2.5 years.
source: As expected the populations of fibrocytes and CD8+ T cells, as well as the density of mixed clusters, decreased. These numbers reached levels similar to healthy subjects after approximately 2.5 years, and this time point can, therefore, be considered as the steady state (Figure 9B–E).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9B-E

claim: Blocking CD54 only slightly reduces the density of CD8+ T cells compared to the placebo condition, and has no effect on fibrocyte and mixed cluster densities.
source: Blocking CD54 only slightly reduced the density of CD8+ T cells compared to the placebo condition, and had no effect on fibrocyte and mixed cluster densities (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9B

claim: CXCR1/2 inhibition is more potent in the reduction of CD8+ T cells than CD54 inhibition, and it also significantly decreases the density of mixed clusters.
source: CXCR1/2 inhibition was a little bit more potent in the reduction of CD8+ T cells than CD54 inhibition, and it also significantly decreased the density of mixed clusters (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9B

claim: Combining both CD54 and CXCR1/2 inhibition therapies does not strongly enhance the effects.
source: Combining both therapies (CD54 and CXCR1/2 inhibition) did not strongly major the effects (Figure 9B–E).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9B-E
